newsitem.title: UK: Confidence seen ebbing among British Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Confidence seen ebbing among British Conservatives.

text.p: Self-confidence, a vital ingredient for political success, seems to be seeping away among Britain's Conservatives as they gear up for a general election that must be held before the end of May.

Under the surface, many in the ruling party have for months been gloomily contemplating being out of power for the first time since 1979 as public opinion polls have consistently repeated their baleful message of a huge Labour party lead.

But this week, a succession of Conservative members of parliament and right-wing commentators have started to talk openly of defeat at the election Prime Minister John Major is widely expected to call for May 1.

"It's no longer if. It's when...It's Labour will this and Labour will that and never mind the formality of an election," Boris Johnson, a political columnist who will fight a Welsh seat for the Conservatives, wrote in the Daily Telegraph newspaper.
"Oh, come on, let's just say it. The Tories are heading for defeat," said former Conservative MP Matthew Parris in the Times.

The party faithful were furious on Friday when the Conservatives' pre-election rally in Bath, a spa city in western England, was cast deeper into gloom by two MPs who openly discussed what should happen following a defeat.

Edwina Currie, a former junior health minister, said Major should step down immediately as party leader to allow a successor to be chosen, while John Biffen, another former minister, said he should stay on as the defeat could be so severe that some would-be leaders lost their parliamentary seats.

Constituency officers who attended the Bath rally loudly applauded when party chairman Brian Mawhinney said in his speech: "To every Conservative, one message -- if you don't have something to say that will help us win, don't say anything at all."
Bath was an odd choice of venue for the pre-election rally.
The beautiful Georgian city was the scene of the party's biggest election upset in 1992 when party chairman Chris Patten, now governor of Hong Kong, lost his seat to the minority Liberal Democrats.
Despite this, some Conservatives who gathered here were still hoping against hope that something would happen in the next 6-1/2 weeks to revive party fortunes.
"We were eight (percentage) points behind in the polls with just a few days to go at the last election," said one. "And we won by eight points. It's happened before, it can happen again."

But privately others are gloomy at polls showing a Labour lead of up to 25 points and following a convincing Labour victory in a previously safe Conservative seat in a parliamentary by-election in northwestern England last month.

"It's ridiculous," said the chairman of one constituency association. "The economy's booming, people have money in their pockets, but they've got it in their heads that it's time for a change of government."
Major tried to stop the rot with a speech outlining plans for a welfare revolution in Britain.
But his task is made more difficult by rival factions behind the scenes who are addressing their minds to the battle to replace him following an election defeat.

Even so, Major seems the Conservatives last great hope. The battle-hardened victor of the 1992 election faces Tony Blair, who, although he has transformed Labour by jettisoning socialist policies, was not even an MP when it was last in power.
"In the last analysis, perhaps people will say 'Better the devil you know', the man who has done it before," said the association chairman. "Maybe that's our best hope."
That is what lies behind Major's choice of the election slogan which he unveiled at Bath: "You can only be sure with the Conservatives."
